ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Cardiology Consultation — Franklin D. Roosevelt — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Two-week heart failure medication safety check and echocardiogram

text.paragraph: New heart failure, probably with reduced ejection fraction and driven by severe hypertension, in a 62-year-old man who smokes and uses a wheelchair. Please review the echocardiogram, confirm the diagnosis and its likely cause, and guide titration of guideline-directed therapy. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two weeks; echocardiogram booked for the morning of the consultation. [S]

list.item: Does the echocardiogram confirm heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and is hypertension a sufficient explanation, or is an ischemic evaluation needed first?
Do you agree with starting all four drug classes at low doses, adding spironolactone after the two-week potassium check, and the order of up-titration?
Should his iron deficiency be treated with intravenous iron?
When should the echocardiogram be repeated, and what would make him a candidate for device therapy?
Is cardiac rehabilitation appropriate for a wheelchair user, and when?

text.paragraph: Mr. Roosevelt is seen at the request of Dr. Brooks two weeks after presenting with breathlessness, orthopnea, and leg swelling. On sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, empagliflozin, and furosemide he is less breathless: he now propels his wheelchair the length of a long corridor before resting and sleeps on two pillows without waking breathless. His home weight has fallen by about 3 kg and his home blood pressures run in the 140s over 80s. He has had no chest pain or pressure at rest or with exertion, no palpitations, no syncope, and no lightheadedness on transfers. He stopped smoking on his quit date last week. His work is demanding and he wants to keep doing it. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on January 30, 1882, at Springwood, the family's estate in Hyde Park, New York. [D]

In the summer of 1921 Roosevelt developed a paralytic illness at Campobello; on August 25, 1921, Dr. Robert Lovett diagnosed infantile paralysis (polio), and Roosevelt remained paraplegic, using leg braces from early 1922. [D]

A 2003 Bayesian analysis of the recorded symptoms concluded that Guillain-Barré syndrome was more probable than paralytic polio as the cause of Roosevelt's 1921 illness; the conclusion is disputed and cannot be confirmed because no cerebrospinal fluid was examined. [R]
In May 1941 Roosevelt had severe iron deficiency anemia, with hemoglobin reported at 4.5 g/100 mL. [D]

At an examination at Bethesda Naval Hospital on March 27, 1944, Roosevelt's blood pressure was 186/108; he was breathless and cyanotic with rales, and X-rays and an electrocardiogram showed an enlarged heart, congestive heart failure, and a mitral murmur. His blood pressure had not been checked since February 27, 1941. [D]

After the March 1944 examination Roosevelt was treated with digitalis, a low-sodium and weight-reduction diet, and rest; his working hours were reduced, his cigarettes were limited to ten a day, and his evening cocktails were reduced. [D]
Roosevelt's father, James Roosevelt, died in 1900 during Franklin's first term at Harvard; his mother, Sara Delano Roosevelt, died at Springwood in September 1941. [D]

list.item: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (I50.22). Confirmed: ejection fraction 30 percent with a dilated, globally hypokinetic left ventricle. He is improving but still mildly congested; NYHA class II to III. Potassium 4.8 mmol/L and creatinine 1.29 mg/dL (eGFR 63) after two weeks of therapy, a rise well within what is accepted, so titration can proceed. [S]

Hypertensive heart disease (I11.0). Severe hypertension, with a presenting blood pressure of 186/108 mmHg and albuminuria, is the most likely cause. There is no angina and no regional wall motion abnormality, so an ischemic evaluation can wait to see whether the ejection fraction recovers with blood pressure control and therapy. Blood pressure 148/88 mmHg today remains above the 130/80 target. [S]

Iron deficiency in heart failure (D50.9). Ferritin 48 ng/mL with transferrin saturation 16 percent meets the heart failure criteria for intravenous iron, which improves symptoms and exercise capacity; oral iron does not. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Today's transthoracic echocardiogram: dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis and no regional wall motion abnormality, ejection fraction 30 percent, and no significant valve disease. Today's basic metabolic panel, the NT-proBNP, iron studies, lipid panel, HbA1c, and TSH from the referral visit. No ECG from the diagnostic workup is on file. [S]

list.item: Increase sacubitril/valsartan to 49/51 mg twice daily and carvedilol to 6.25 mg twice daily with food today. [S]
Start spironolactone 25 mg daily today; potassium 4.8 mmol/L and eGFR 63 allow it. [S]
Continue empagliflozin 10 mg daily, and furosemide 20 mg daily until he is euvolemic. [S]
Basic metabolic panel one to two weeks after today's changes. [S]
Ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg intravenously today and again in one week. [S]

Ischemic evaluation, with pharmacologic stress imaging or coronary CT angiography because he cannot exercise on a treadmill, only if the ejection fraction does not improve on therapy or angina develops. [S]

Repeat echocardiogram three to six months after tolerated doses are reached. An implantable defibrillator is indicated only if the ejection fraction is still 35 percent or less after at least three months of therapy; obtain an ECG before that decision to measure the QRS duration. [S]
Cardiac rehabilitation once he has had six weeks of therapy, in a program that offers seated arm ergometry and resistance training. [S]
Stay off cigarettes; keep alcohol to an occasional drink. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Brooks in person today; the patient agrees with the plan. [S]

Follow-up: Primary care will manage the titration and laboratory monitoring on the CMID schedule. Cardiology will see him again for an ejection fraction that stays at 35 percent or less, a failure to improve, new angina or arrhythmia, or a hospital admission. [S]
